statement: Maya script decipherment was a decades-long collaborative process, not a single breakthrough. J. Eric S. Thompson dominated the field into the 1960s championing a purely ideographic, non-phonetic, non-historical reading of the script and rejected Yuri Knorozov's 1952 phonetic (logogram + CV-syllable) argument until Thompson's own death in 1975; Cold War-era politics around Knorozov's Soviet nationality are documented (though not to full academic-historiography rigor in this pass) as a real contributing factor in the delay. Tatiana Proskouriakoff ("Historical Implications of a Pattern of Dates at Piedras Negras, Guatemala," American Antiquity 25(4), 1960, pp. 454-475) demonstrated that stelae date-patterns recorded real dynastic events of named rulers, overturning Thompson's purely calendrical/religious reading. Linda Schele, Floyd Lounsbury, Peter Mathews, David Stuart, and Nikolai Grube completed the collaborative phonetic/logosyllabic decipherment through the 1970s-1990s. Current status: DECIPHERED, with roughly 80-90% of signs/inscriptions readable per David Stuart (University of Texas) — core grammar solved, but a nontrivial minority of rare/unique signs and some toponyms remain unread or contested; do not report as 100% solved.
